rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The midpoint temperature leaves room to probe selectivity in either direction.
Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test a faster method while retaining full resolution, keeping injection 1 as the proven optimum.
The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF, but the critical pair has little resolution margin. Increase temperature one step to test whether selectivity improves while further reducing retention time.

Test a further gradient shortening with a modest temperature increase, which has so far improved the critical pair’s selectivity. This probes the speed limit while preserving the previously demonstrated maximum-CRF methods as fallbacks.
Lower phi1 to make the six-minute gradient shallower and recover resolution of the critical pair. The previous last peak exited near 0.53 organic fraction, so 0.80 leaves ample elution headroom.

Shift the gradient window upward while keeping its slope unchanged to remove time spent at weak solvent strength. This tests whether the maximum CRF can be retained with earlier elution; the first peak previously exited near 0.21 organic fraction.

Slightly flatten the shifted gradient to restore the critical pair from R = 1.42 to full resolution. This should retain much of injection 6’s time saving relative to the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Trim the gradient window and shorten its duration, using a slightly shallower slope to protect the critical pair. The previous last peak exited near 0.51 organic fraction, so the new endpoint should still allow complete elution.

Increase the endpoint by one grid step to shorten elution while testing the critical pair’s remaining resolution margin. Keep the starting composition and temperature fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

Raise temperature one step to test whether its favorable effect on the middle critical pair restores full resolution at this faster slope. Monitor the first pair closely because its resolution decreased with warming in earlier runs.

Return to 50 C to protect the first pair, and raise the starting organic fraction to reduce retention time. The narrower gradient window provides a shallower slope to help preserve middle-pair resolution.

Maximum CRF is already secured; test a much steeper gradient for a faster, alternative separation after a possible middle-pair order reversal. Lower temperature and starting organic fraction should help protect the early pair from compression.

Test the low-temperature extreme at the same steep slope to measure whether temperature can separate the reordered middle pair. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates selectivity changes in this fast-elution regime.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves the middle-pair separation in the steep-gradient regime. A relatively low temperature should help retain and separate the earliest compounds, though early compression remains a risk.

Probe a narrow, high-organic window at low temperature for an alternative fast separation. This tests starting-composition selectivity beyond the unsuccessful broad, steep gradients, while the maximum-CRF methods remain established fallbacks.

Shift the previous window upward at unchanged slope to test whether starting-composition selectivity can resolve the middle pair. This is exploratory: the first peak is already nearly unretained, so early-pair compression may limit this approach.

Keep the starting composition fixed to protect the first pair, and halve the gradient slope to test whether the middle pair gains the remaining resolution. The previous last peak exited near 0.61 organic fraction, so some final-hold elution is expected.

Test a near-isocratic early separation to see whether further flattening resolves the middle pair while preserving the first pair. This sacrifices some speed to establish whether the high-starting-organic regime can reach full resolution.

Return to the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF region and lower the endpoint one step to increase resolution margin over injection 11. The high-starting-organic experiments showed too little middle-pair improvement to justify further slowing that regime.

Test a higher starting composition to shorten retention, with a shallower slope to support middle-pair resolution. Lowering temperature to 45 C should help protect the early pair against compression from the stronger starting solvent.

Use a slope between injections 8 and 9 to approach the fastest fully resolved separation without increasing the starting solvent strength. This should recover the middle pair above R = 1.5 while retaining adequate early-pair resolution.

Refine around injection 11 with a slightly shallower slope to increase its narrow middle-pair resolution margin. This targets a fully resolved separation near 3.5 minutes while retaining the demonstrated maximum CRF.

Test a cooler neighbor of injection 8 to improve early-pair separation while checking that the middle pair retains full resolution. With maximum CRF already secured, this evaluates a potentially more balanced resolution margin at a small time cost.

Flatten injection 8’s gradient by one endpoint step to increase the middle-pair resolution margin while preserving early retention. This targets a more balanced, fully resolved method with only a modest time increase and no expected CRF penalty.

Use the final injection to test a four-minute gradient near the proven maximum-CRF region, with a weaker starting solvent to retain the earliest peaks. Its slope is slightly shallower than injection 7’s, supporting full resolution while keeping elution comfortably below ten minutes.
